intro.html: Five small Greek and Latin prefixes unlock this topic. Two mean all: Latin omni- and Greek pan-. Ambi- means both. Greek eu- means good or well (and its opposite, dys-, means bad). Hyper- means over or beyond.
You already know these prefixes from everyday words: omnivore (eats all), panorama (a view of all), ambidextrous (good with both hands), hyperactive (over-active).

words.ex: In the fairy tale, the {omnipotent} wizard could turn mountains into marbles with a wave of his wand.
words.ctx: The young king believed he was {omnipotent}, but the flood soon taught him that even a ruler cannot order the rain to stop.
words.etym: From Latin omnipotens: omnis (all) + potens (able, powerful).

mn.text: In Pip’s daydream he lifts a whole house with one finger and waves away the rain clouds; he imagines he is {omnipotent}.

scene.alt: A boy in a cape holds a whole house up on one finger and blows the rain clouds away.

words.def: knowing everything there is to know
words.ex: The story is told by an {omniscient} narrator who knows every character’s secret thoughts.
words.ctx: Grandma seemed {omniscient} to us kids: she always knew who had eaten the cookies, who had tracked in the mud and who had skipped brushing their teeth.
words.etym: From Latin omnis (all) + sciens (knowing), the root of science.

mn.text: With her back to the room, Granny Mae says, “Pip, put that cookie back.” She knows everything that happens in her kitchen; she seems {omniscient}.

scene.alt: A grandmother with her back turned catches her grandson sneaking a cookie.

words.def: a cure for all problems or illnesses
words.ex: A new phone is no {panacea} for boredom.
words.ctx: The new reading program helped many students, but the teachers warned that it was no {panacea}: some children still needed extra help with spelling, and others simply needed glasses.
words.note: Panacea is most often used in the negative: “no panacea,” “not a panacea.”

mn.cue: PAN-ACEA: one PAN that cures ALL?
mn.text: A traveling seller swears his shiny frying pan cures colds, sadness and bad grades; nobody believes in a {panacea} like that.

scene.alt: A seller holds up a shiny frying pan under a sign claiming it cures everything, while a woman frowns.

words.ex: When the mouse ran across the cafeteria, {pandemonium} broke out.
words.ctx: The quiet library turned to {pandemonium} when the alarm went off: chairs scraped, books tumbled and everyone rushed for the doors at once.
words.etym: Coined in 1667 by the poet John Milton as the name of the demons’ capital in his long poem: pan- (all) + Late Latin daemonium (evil spirit). The sense “wild uproar” came later.

mn.text: A mouse dashes across the kitchen; the cat leaps, every pan clatters to the floor, and everyone shrieks at once. The kitchen is {pandemonium}.

scene.alt: A mouse runs across a kitchen as a cat leaps, pans fly and people scream.

words.def: having mixed feelings, pulled two ways at once
words.ex: Lila felt {ambivalent} about moving: excited to see a new city but sad to leave her friends.
words.ctx: He was {ambivalent} about the job offer; the pay was wonderful, but the long commute would mean seeing his children only on weekends.
words.etym: Made from ambi- (both) + Latin valens (being strong): feelings that are strong in both directions.
words.note: Ambivalent means pulled two ways at once, not uninterested. Someone who does not care either way is indifferent.

mn.text: Pip wants to go to the beach and wants to go to the movies just as much; pulled both ways at once, he is {ambivalent}.

scene.alt: A boy shrugs between a sign pointing to the beach and a sign pointing to the movies, pulled both ways.

words.def: able to be understood in more than one way
words.ex: Her {ambiguous} reply, “We’ll see,” could have meant yes or no.
words.ctx: The note was {ambiguous}: “Meet me at the bank” could mean the bank on Main Street or the riverbank behind the school.
words.etym: From Latin ambiguus, “uncertain,” from ambigere (to waver): ambi- (around, both ways) + agere (to drive).

mn.cue: the BANK? or the river BANK?
mn.text: Kai’s note says “Meet me at the bank,” so Lila waits at the riverbank while Kai waits at the money bank; the note was {ambiguous}.

labels.text: AMBI: TWO WAYS to read it

scene.alt: A girl waits at a riverbank reading a note that says bank, unsure whether it means the river or the city bank.

words.def: a gentle word used in place of a harsh or blunt one
words.ctx: The company called the layoffs “rightsizing,” a {euphemism} meant to make the loss of two hundred jobs sound like a sensible adjustment.

roots.means: a practice, a way of doing

words.etym: From Greek euphemismos, from euphemos (speaking well): eu (well) + pheme (speech).

mn.cue: EU = GOOD: a nice word for a bad thing
mn.text: Grandpa Gus calls his rusty, smoking old car “a classic.” That kind word for a wreck is a {euphemism}.

scene.alt: A grandfather proudly calls his smoking, rusty old car a classic while a girl giggles.

words.def: a speech or writing in praise of someone, especially someone who has died
words.ex: Grandpa’s oldest friend gave a warm {eulogy}, full of funny stories, at his memorial.
words.ctx: Rather than list the scientist’s awards, the {eulogy} described her kindness: the students she fed, the letters she answered and the neighbors she helped.
words.note: A eulogy (praise) is not an elegy (a sad poem or song).

mn.cue: EU-LOGY: GOOD WORDS about a life
mn.text: At the memorial, Maya steps to the podium and shares warm, funny stories about her grandfather’s life; her speech of praise is a {eulogy}.

scene.alt: A teen at a podium shares kind memories of her grandfather beside flowers and a framed picture.

words.ex: “I’ve told you a million times” is {hyperbole}.
words.ctx: When Jonah said his backpack weighed a ton, he was using {hyperbole}; it was heavy, but he carried it the whole mile to school.
words.etym: From Greek hyperbole, “excess,” from hyperballein (to throw beyond): hyper (beyond) + ballein (to throw).

mn.cue: HYPER: words thrown way OVER the top
mn.text: Jonah staggers in with a small backpack, groaning, “This weighs a TON! I’m dying!” His over-the-top words are {hyperbole}.

scene.alt: A teen groans that his small backpack weighs a ton while his friend laughs.

words.def: an imagined society where life is miserable and people are not free
words.ex: The novel is set in a gray {dystopia} where no one is allowed to sing.
words.ctx: Unlike the cheerful future in her first book, her new story imagines a {dystopia}: a crowded city where every word is recorded and no one dares to laugh.
words.etym: Made from dys- (bad) + utopia, the name of an ideal land, from Greek ou (not) + topos (place).

mn.text: In the story, robots patrol gray streets under a sign that says NO SINGING, and nobody smiles; that miserable imagined world is a {dystopia}.

scene.alt: On a gray, rainy street, two sad people pass a patrolling robot and a sign that says no singing.

after.html: Keep the pairs apart: ambivalent (mixed feelings) is about how you feel; ambiguous (two possible meanings) is about what something says. And a eulogy praises, while an elegy mourns.

items.q: Mia wants to join the team but dreads the early practices. She feels…
items.why: Pulled two ways at once is ambivalent. Indifferent means not caring at all; ambiguous describes words with two meanings.

items.q: A speech praising someone who has died is a…
items.why: A eulogy is a speech of praise (eu = good, logos = word). An elegy is a sad poem.

items.q: True or false: “My backpack weighs a ton” is an example of hyperbole.
items.why: True. It is a deliberate exaggeration: hyper (over) + ballein (to throw).
eu- means good or well (euphemism, eulogy); dys- means bad (dystopia).
